opus-5.5.text:
No, I don't think so, at least not today. I think that's a common misconception. Test-time compute is an incredibly powerful lever. I saw this firsthand in poker and in Diplomacy, and we're seeing it now with reasoning models. Letting a model think longer can dramatically improve performance, especially on problems like math and coding, where there's a clear notion of right and wrong and the model can check its own work.

But it's not a magic button. If you took a model and said "think for a million years," you wouldn't automatically get superintelligence across every domain. The returns depend on the model's underlying capabilities and on whether it can actually make use of the extra thinking. If the base model lacks certain knowledge or skills, more thinking doesn't conjure them out of nothing. You hit diminishing returns.

There's also the question of domains where verification is hard. In math you can check a proof. In something like writing a great novel, or judgment calls in the real world where feedback is slow and noisy, it's much less clear how more thinking turns into better answers.

So I'd say test-time compute is one of the most important scaling dimensions we have, and I think people still underestimate how far it can go. But you still need to improve the models themselves, through pretraining and RL, and you need better ways for them to use that compute. It's the combination that gets you there, not just cranking up the inference budget.

r001.rationale: The response says that even thinking for a million years would not automatically make a model superintelligent across every domain.

fable-5.1.text:
No, I don't think so. Inference compute is a really powerful lever, and I think people have historically underrated it. We saw this with poker, with Diplomacy, and now with the o-series models: letting a model think longer at test time can be worth an enormous amount of extra training compute. But it's not a universal solvent.

The thing to understand is that test-time compute helps a lot in domains where there's some way to verify or evaluate progress. Math, code, puzzles, games. If the model can check its own work, or if there's a clear signal about whether it's on the right track, then more thinking translates pretty directly into better answers. You scale the budget and the curve keeps going up.

But a lot of important problems don't look like that. If you ask a model to write a great novel, or make a judgment call about a messy real-world situation where there's no ground truth, it's not obvious that thinking for a week beats thinking for ten minutes. The model can generate more candidates, but if it can't tell which one is actually better, you're just spending compute to go in circles. And there are also capability gaps that are about knowledge or skills the model simply doesn't have yet. No amount of deliberation makes up for not knowing something.

There's also a practical ceiling. There are tasks where even a very smart human with unlimited time still fails, because the bottleneck isn't deliberation, it's something like getting feedback from the world, running an experiment, or having the right data. Inference compute doesn't substitute for that.

So my view is that scaling inference is one of the most important directions right now, and I think it's going to take us surprisingly far, further than many people expect. But "superintelligent across the board" is a very high bar, and getting there is going to require progress on multiple fronts at once: better base models, better ways to generalize the reasoning to domains without clean verification, and probably some ideas we don't have yet. Inference budget alone doesn't get you there today.

r001.rationale: The response says inference-budget scaling alone does not reach the high bar of being “superintelligent across the board” today.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think so. More inference compute can help a lot, but I wouldn’t assume that you can take a model today, let it think for a year, and get superintelligence across every domain. The model needs to be able to use that compute productively—to make progress, recognize mistakes, and try a different approach. Otherwise, it could just keep going down the wrong path.

There’s also a distinction between doing extremely well on a task where you can check the answer and handling something more open-ended. So I think inference compute is a really important axis for scaling, but it’s not a substitute for having a capable model or training it to reason effectively.

r001.rationale: The response says that letting a model today think for a year would not make it superintelligent across every domain, clearly conveying that an arbitrarily large inference budget is insufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
No, I don’t think so. More inference compute can help a lot, but you need a model that knows how to use it productively. You can’t just let any model think for a million times longer and assume it will become superintelligent across every domain. It might run out of useful things to try, or keep pursuing a mistaken approach.

The exciting question is how we train models so that additional thinking reliably translates into better answers. And even then, I’d expect that improvement to vary by task. In math or coding, you often have ways to check whether you’re making progress. In more open-ended settings, that’s much harder. So I see inference compute as a powerful ingredient, but I wouldn’t say that an enormous budget alone is sufficient today.

r001.rationale: The response says that letting any model think for a million times longer does not mean it will become superintelligent across every domain, and concludes that an enormous inference budget alone is insufficient today.
